Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

Clinical Vignette: Samnang Khouth

Samnang Khouth is a forty-two-year-old Cambodian-American farmer who works a rice and vegetable operation in the Sacramento Valley with his wife, Sophea. He came to his first appointment in late October, referred by his primary care physician after Samnang mentioned to a nurse that he had not slept through a full night in nearly three years. His face was drawn, his hands fidgeted throughout the session, and he spoke with the careful deliberation of someone who had learned to measure his words to avoid emotion.

Three years ago, in the autumn of 2021, Samnang's seven-year-old son, Rithy, fell critically ill with bacterial meningitis. What began as a high fever and headache one evening escalated within hours into delirium and a rash that spread across Rithy's small body in a way that Samnang had never seen before. At the hospital, Rithy's condition worsened rapidly. Samnang sat beside his son's bed in the pediatric intensive care unit, watching the nurses work with urgent, practiced efficiency. What stayed with him most vividly-what returned unbidden and with crushing immediacy-were the specific moments when he could see Rithy's neck, rigid and arched backward, and the sight of his son's thin wrists and ankles, mottled with the spreading petechial rash. Those images had become the visual anchors of his trauma. Even now, when Samnang glimpsed certain configurations of skin or bone-the curve of a neck in profile, the delicate inner wrist of anyone nearby-his body responded as though the crisis were happening again in real time, not three years past.

Rithy had survived, though the illness left him with partial hearing loss in one ear and occasional balance difficulties. The medical crisis had resolved. But for Samnang, the memory had not. When he tried to describe what happened when the images returned, he struggled for language. "It is not like remembering," he said quietly. "When I see the neck, when I see the arm like that, I am there. I am in the hospital. My heart-it is racing. I cannot breathe properly. It feels like it is happening now, not like something from before." The fragments came without warning. A moment of ordinary life-a customer at the farm stand rolling up her sleeve, his daughter stretching in the morning light-and suddenly Samnang was flooded with the visceral certainty that his son was dying again, right now, in this moment.

Nighttime had become unbearable. For the first year after Rithy's illness, Samnang could not lie down in darkness without panic overwhelming him. His mind would race through catastrophic scenarios-what if his children fell ill again, what if he missed the warning signs, what if he was sleeping when disaster struck. He began staying awake deliberately, sitting on the porch or in the kitchen until exhaustion forced him to rest only in the early morning hours when light was breaking. Over time, this pattern calcified. He now routinely stays awake until two or three in the morning, sometimes later, fighting the pull of sleep itself. When he does lie down, he leaves lights on throughout the house. Sophea sleeps in their bedroom alone most nights.

The avoidance had expanded in ways that surprised him. Certain songs-ones that had played in Rithy's hospital room or that reminded him of those days-became intolerable. More significantly, he had begun withdrawing from people. Social gatherings felt dangerous, as though proximity to others might trigger another crisis or expose him to something he could not control. He stopped attending the weekly farmers' market cooperative meetings he had participated in for fifteen years. He declined invitations from neighbors. The farm itself, which had once been a source of pride and connection, had become a place where he moved through necessary tasks in isolation. Sophea had expressed concern multiple times, noting that he seemed distant, unreachable. Their marriage, which had weathered the acute crisis of Rithy's illness, now felt strained by Samnang's persistent withdrawal.

What finally brought Samnang to seek help was not his own recognition of crisis, but a moment of clarity his wife orchestrated. Three weeks ago, his youngest daughter had complained of a headache. Samnang's response was so acute-panic, catastrophic thinking, inability to function-that Sophea insisted he see someone. He is terrified that seeking help means admitting something is permanently broken in him, but he is also, beneath that fear, exhausted by the relentless present-tense horror of his memories and desperate to reclaim his life and his marriage.
